articles.title: Destroyer That Has Been Deployed Longer Than Any Since WWII Returns Home
articles.text:
Two guided-missile destroyers assigned to the Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group (CSG), USS Spruance and USS Michael Murphy, have returned home after 357- and 346-day deployments, respectively, more than a month after the carrier they escorted returned to San Diego. Both are reportedly longer than any previous destroyer cruise since World War II. However, the record may not hold for long, as USS John Finn is on pace to surpass both.

Spruance pulled out of Naval Base San Diego on November 21, 2025, alongside Nimitz class aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln, on what the crews expected would be a routine deployment to the Western Pacific. Murphy linked up with the strike group 10 days later as it sailed past her homeport at Joint Base Pearl Harbor-Hickam, Hawaii.

Both ships, which endured conditions just as grueling as Lincoln, if not more so, returned to their homeports over the past 24 hours. Spruance departed Pearl Harbor on November 6, according to MarineTraffic, and arrived in San Diego today. Planet Labs satellite imagery reviewed by TWZ showed Murphy in Guam on November 3, her last stop before transiting northeast back to Pearl Harbor and pulling into port yesterday.

The extended deployments are a reminder of how the war with Iran and the blockade that followed have pushed the Navy’s surface fleet past the seven-month cruises it long treated as standard. Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told Sailors recently to expect the new normal for deployments to last 10 months, at a minimum, going forward.

Spruance’s deployment is the longest since World War II by a destroyer, based on a report by the San Diego Union-Tribune that cited the Navy, and broke the record previously held by USS McFaul, which returned to Norfolk on October 23 after 332 days. TWZ has not been able to independently verify the paper’s sourcing on the WWII comparison. When asked about the record, Naval History and Heritage Command told Stars and Stripes that it “does not officially track or verify superlative claims such as ‘the longest deployment’ for a destroyer.”

Before 2020, destroyer deployments rarely exceeded nine months. USS Stout’s pandemic cruise included a record-setting 215 consecutive days at sea and was among the longest in the modern era at 269 days. Since then, USS Gravely and USS Mason, while escorting carrier USS Dwight D. Eisenhower in 2023 and 2024 during combat operations against the Houthi, were out for 275 and 263 days, respectively.

Notably, Spruance and Murphy have been deployed even longer than any aircraft carrier since the Vietnam War, surpassing the 326-day record set by USS Gerald R. Ford in May. Ford’s high mark could fall again, though, as Navy leaders recently told families of USS George H.W. Bush at a town hall to plan for a yearlong deployment if the blockade continues or war with Iran restarts.

What Part Did USS Spruance And USS Michael Murphy Play In The Iran War?

As part of the Abraham Lincoln CSG, which also included USS Frank E. Petersen Jr. serving as the Integrated Air and Missile Defense (IAMD) Commander, Spruance and Murphy were instrumental in the opening act of Operation Epic Fury, the nearly 40 days of combat operations that followed, and both rounds of the blockade.

Spruance was spotted firing a never-before-seen black Tomahawk Land Attack Missile (TLAM) on February 28, the first night of the war, and later fired rounds from her Mk 45 5-inch gun into the engine room of an Iranian-flagged container ship to prevent it from running the blockade – a first in nearly four decades. Murphy was the last U.S. warship out of the Persian Gulf before hostilities kicked off, docking in Dubai from February 25 to 27, and also launched salvos of TLAMs at land targets on Iran’s southern flank.

While Spruance’s cruise has drawn media attention, Murphy’s accomplishments have received little to no recognition.

Murphy and Petersen Jr. were the first warships to transit back through the Strait of Hormuz after major combat operations ended in April. Open-source intelligence indicated the two destroyers came under heavy enemy fire during the maneuver. Capt. Casey Mahon, the commanding officer of Petersen Jr., told reporters at the ship’s homecoming that the strait transit was “Quite a voyage… obviously there was stress we had to face when we did that… on the sea, under the sea, and in the air.”

“In recognition of extraordinary heroism and combat achievement while executing dozens of Tomahawk land-attack cruise missile strikes and defending against hostile drone and missile attacks, USS Michael Murphy and its crew were awarded the Presidential Unit Citation and the Combat Action Ribbon,” a press release from U.S. 3rd Fleet announced.

When Lincoln began the long trip home and stopped in Thailand after setting a record for the most consecutive days at sea without a liberty port call, Spruance and Murphy were left behind in the U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility (AOR) to continue enforcing blockade measures. Petersen Jr., due to her role as IAMD Commander, accompanied the carrier during the visit, as did guided-missile cruiser USS Robert Smalls for additional air defense coverage.

Could USS John Finn Break USS Spruance’s Record?

Spruance’s record might not stand for long. USS John Finn, a destroyer based out of Yokosuka, Japan, part of the Forward Deployed Naval Forces (FDNF), got underway on January 9, 2026. The crew expected a routine three-month patrol in the Western Pacific, which is typical for warships assigned to FDNF, but the ship was redirected to the CENTCOM AOR, where she’s been since the start of the war. The Sailors were informed in October to expect to return in March 2027, according to a report by Defense One. If that timeline plays out, Finn would pass Spruance at year-end 2026 and log over 400 days deployed (13 to 14 months).

“You can kind of expect at least a 10-month deployment, and so that’s just the nature of what the capacity of the Navy can do,” Caudle said at the U.S. Navy Memorial Special Edition SITREP Series on October 26. “I need a bigger Navy,” he added. The total battle force today sits at just over 280 warships, with approximately 78 destroyers in various states of readiness.

Two other destroyers forward-stationed in Yokosuka, USS Rafael Peralta and USS Mustin, have been told to expect to return in April 2027, according to the report by Defense One. Peralta left port on March 9 after returning home for a brief three weeks following a seven-week patrol; Mustin departed on April 14 on a surge deployment that was supposed to end in August. If that’s the case, both will approach or surpass the one-year mark.

How Do Extended Deployments Impact The Navy?

Caudle also warned that the destroyer fleet faces a problematic maintenance backlog when the ships return home after such a long period of time at sea. “You’re talking hundreds of availabilities and millions of dollars,” he said. “But this is a years-long recovery. There is no workaround on that.” That backlog would still be working its way through the yards if a contingency in Asia arose in the next few years.

The impact of intense combat operations was apparent when Lincoln pulled into Thailand looking worse for wear with running rust and algae along the hull.

Spruance’s next maintenance period was originally scheduled to begin in July but has now been pushed to January 2027, based on budget documents reviewed by TWZ.

Open-ended deployments also weigh on the morale of Sailors and take a toll on their families and friends back home. “We are hearing they’re supposed to come home sometime next month, but we’ve been hearing about ‘next month’ for several months,” a family member of a Sailor aboard Spruance told Navy Times in late October. Speaking anonymously, a Sailor on the ship told the outlet, “Our boat isn’t as big as an aircraft carrier, but our 300-plus families matter to us just as much as anyone else’s.”

In recent decades, as mentioned above, a typical deployment has lasted six to seven months. “That commitment is being violated now,” Katherine Kuzminski, a vice president at the Center for a New American Security, told Defense One. The issue for Sailors and families, she explained, is the “dissonance between what was said at the beginning and what is happening in actuality.” A spouse of a Sailor aboard Finn told the outlet, “I can do a long deployment. The problem with this is that there is no answer as to when this will be over.”

The Navy did not announce either homecoming date publicly in advance.

Spruance began broadcasting AIS again on November 11 but was holding roughly 50 nautical miles northwest of San Diego. U.S. Navy Patrol escorted Spruance in to the port with a two-boat security element just after 9 a.m. local time today. Murphy switched her AIS on south of Hawaii yesterday, an hour and a half before arriving in Pearl Harbor.

To the crews of both ships: welcome home.

articles.title: OpenAI board member worries an AI "takeover" of society could be months away
articles.text:
How do you think you're going to die?

If you go by the current statistics for deaths in the US, it's reasonable to expect that cancer or heart disease will eventually get you. But OpenAI Foundation board member and Alignment Research Center Executive Director Paul Cristiano thinks we should all be worried about another major mortality risk. Speaking at a lecture series this week, Cristiano bluntly told the audience in a Toronto Convention Center, "I think for most people in this room, the most likely reason they will die is because of an AI accident."

In the opening lecture of a three-part series, Cristiano outlined his worries about the risk of an impending "AI takeover." He defined that as a situation where goal-pursuing AI systems "call the shots in the same sense that humans today call the shots and what happens on Earth" and where any human trying to stop them "would be as ineffective as if you or me was trying to stop the US military." Such a situation would likely lead to mass death and perhaps uninhabitable environments for humans, Cristiano said.

articles.title: B-21 Raider Has Released Its First Weapon
articles.text:
The B-21 Raider has released a weapon for the first time as testing of the bomber continues to expand in scale and scope. This is a new and significant step forward for the B-21, which the U.S. Air Force hopes will begin its operational service in 2027.

The Air Force and Northrop Grumman announced the start of B-21 weapons testing in separate press releases.

“During the test, a B-21 test aircraft flying from Edwards Air Force Base, California, released a conventional weapon, validating its digital models and the maturity of its open systems architecture,” according to the Air Force. “This test proves the B-21’s strike capability, proves its ability to rapidly onboard new weapons and solidifies its role as the future backbone of the U.S. bomber fleet.”

The Air Force’s release does not name the munition in question or provide any more context about the release. The B-21 is intended to carry a wide variety of conventional and nuclear munitions. The still-in-development AGM-181A Long Range Stand-Off (LRSO) nuclear-armed cruise missile is set to be a particularly key part of the Raider’s arsenal.

At the time of writing, no images of the bomber actually dropping anything have been released. From what has been seen previously, the B-21 looks to have a single large central weapons bay compared to the two side-by-side bays on the existing B-2 Spirit. The possibility has been raised in the past that the Raider could also have smaller secondary bays, but visual evidence to date doesn’t point conclusively to this being the case.

As the B-21 is also smaller than the B-2, the Raider has a lower gross payload capacity by tonnage. How much less remains unclear. Satellite imagery recently confirmed that the B-21 is nowhere near as diminutive compared to the B-2 as many had previously estimated.

“The execution of the test was built on thousands of hours of virtual modeling within the B-21’s digital twin environment,” the Air Force’s release adds. “This allowed the B-21 Combined Test Force to accelerate weapons integration and predict and refine the weapon’s trajectory with unparalleled precision before the aircraft ever left the ground.”

The Air Force is currently known to have two flying pre-production Raiders out of a planned test force of six aircraft. The service has said in the past that it plans to acquire at least 100 B-21s, but a new target fleet size figure is expected to be released next year. The Air Force and Northrop Grumman announced plans to accelerate production of the bombers earlier this year.

It is interesting to note that the B-2 first flew in 1989 and conducted its first weapons release in 1992, which is similar to the timeline we’ve now seen with the B-21. However, the B-2 did not reach initial operational capability (IOC) until 1997.

While it seems relatively late in the process in relation to the scheduled fielding of the aircraft set to come next year for the B-21 to have only just started weapons testing now, the Raider’s development was always going to be different. Much of this is attributed to digital engineering and having the first aircraft highly representative of production models. Still, with just two aircraft in the air, moving from first weapons release to IOC within a year is clearly an aggressive ask.

“This weapons test proves the B-21 program is excelling,” Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Ken Wilsbach said in a statement today. “We are building an impressive fleet that will give our joint force credible, penetrating strike options for decades to come.”

The Air Force, as well as members of Congress, have consistently described the B-21 program as a model acquisition effort in terms of staying on schedule and on budget, despite hurdles in the past. The testing regime has been steadily expanding since the Raider first flew in 2023. Tests over the past year have been increasingly geared toward validating key operational capabilities, including the aircraft’s ability to refuel in-flight.

“The B-21 is proving in test what it promised on paper: it’s the most advanced bomber in the fleet, and it behaves more like a modern fighter than a legacy bomber when it comes to maintenance turnaround times and cost per flying hour,” Northrop Grumman says in its press release today. “The B-21 is setting new benchmarks in materiel reliability, weapons loading and rapid data collection – all strong indicators it’s on track to be a true daily flyer.”

“Northrop Grumman has already completed lifetimes of fatigue testing months ahead of schedule, further validating the strength and resilience of the B-21’s design,” the company’s release adds. “On the flight line, the combined test team is pushing a robust tempo in alignment with the Department of War’s call to operate on solid wartime footing. Each sortie adds to a growing body of data and confidence, moving the B-21 one step closer to joining the operational fleet.”

Air Force officials have also settled on how the B-21 will be crewed during operational missions, with two pilots in the cockpit. The service announced in June that an operational test pilot, rather than a developmental one, had flown a Raider for the first time.

“The B-21 Raider offers exceptional payload flexibility, giving commanders the ability to tailor weapon loadouts to a wide range of mission requirements, from long-range strikes to operations in heavily defended airspace,” Northrop Grumman also notes in its release. “B-21 is also adaptable by design, allowing new weapons and capabilities to be integrated over time, keeping it ahead of evolving threats and maintaining its role as a pacing sixth-generation system.”

It is worth noting here that the Air Force has described the B-21 as also having multi-mission capabilities that go beyond air-to-ground/surface strike. The service confirmed last month that this could potentially extend into the air-to-air combat arena. The expectation that the Raider would be much more than just a bomber is something TWZ had been highlighting for years before the aircraft was even unveiled.

More about the Air Force’s plans for employing its B-21 fleet could well continue to emerge as the service gets closer to fielding the Raider. The groundwork is already being laid for the scheduled arrival of the first operational B-21s at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota next year.

“The B-21 is designed to deliver improved combat capability to the warfighter, combining reliability and maintainability to quickly integrate new weapons,” Secretary of the Air Force Troy Meink said in a statement today. “This successful test demonstrates our ability to adapt rapidly and hold any target at risk if deterrence fails.”

articles.title: Mozilla leaves Solo website owners to go it alone as hosting shuts down
articles.text:
Solo, Mozilla's LLM-powered website builder and hosting service, is shutting down. All sites and data will be deleted on November 30.

Mozilla launched Solo in December 2023 as a "Mozilla Innovation Project," aimed at helping sole traders to build themselves a webpage for their services. Some 54,000 people used its LLM to build pages, and relied on Mozilla to host them – complete with custom domain names.

Well, not any more. Now the Soloist.ai homepage says: "We've made the difficult decision to close Solo. We have appreciated all of your support building and growing this product, and the feedback we've received from all of you. Solo will cease operations on Nov 30, 2026."

Users now have just over two weeks left to find a new home for their pages, although Mozilla says it first notified them on October 1. According to the support FAQ, users can download a ZIP containing an HTML export, contact form and newsletter submissions, and a CSV linking to their images.

The images themselves must be downloaded separately. Domains purchased through Solo Domains must also be moved to Name.com, with Mozilla handling the transfer after users create an account and supply its code. So much for having the fiddly bits taken care of.

It also points at a couple of other bot-based site-generating services – in case all this feels like a bit too much. We suspect that for the sort of technophobes that this was aimed at, it very probably will.

Mozilla told The Register: "Experimentation is an important part of Mozilla's mission to make the internet better and give people more choice and control online. Sometimes, that means making the decision to bring a product to an end. Solo will officially shut down on November 30, 2026. We initially notified customers on October 1, providing a 60-day transition period, and have been offering support to help them download their website data and migrate their domains purchased via Solo Domains to another hosting provider."

It seems that some 54,000 users were not enough to keep it going, and we can see that this would cost money to keep running. An HTML export is a start, though the FAQ doesn't explain how much work it will take to get a complete, functioning site running elsewhere.

Buried in the dark recesses of the web is this vulture's own nearly 30-year-old homepage, created using a mixture of Claris Home Page (which was excellent) and Microsoft FrontPage (ever so slightly less so). We saw what a mess machine-generated web content was back then, and thanks to LLMs, we suspect it is almost infinitely worse now.

Mozilla might have made a few bucks by finding a commercial partner to take on its users, and perhaps through them offer a paid site-and-domain transfer service. As we noted last year, it seems not to have negotiated anything with KaiOSTech, which maintains and sells what used to be the formerly FOSS FirefoxOS for use on low-end smartphones.

articles.title: Email addresses used in European school bomb hoaxes spotted in old infostealer logs
articles.text:
Two email addresses used to send bomb threats that disrupted thousands of Italian schools this week were found exposed in infostealer logs for over a year, experts say.

Researchers at Hudson Rock looked into the two university email addresses used to send the bomb threats. One, from Egypt’s Kafrelsheikh University, was scooped up by Vidar – a cybercrime tool that steals saved account credentials and passwords from an infected computer and leaks them to attackers – as far back as October 2021. The other, from Taiwan's Dayeh University, was found among the 284 million addresses included in the massive AlienTXTBASE infostealer dump, dated February 2025.

The experts said that the two addresses in infostealer logs do not strictly mean that those behind the bomb threats gained access to the accounts using the previous infostealer compromise.

However, it suggests that there was ample time for the universities and Microsoft, which both universities used for authentication, to take action against the accounts that they should have been aware were appearing in infostealer logs.

Modern threat intelligence has made infostealer logs highly visible.

"Both findings place credential exposure well before the disruption, creating a substantial window in which exposed access could have been investigated and secured," Hudson Rock said.

The researchers said that they would need access to details such as the email headers, and data from email providers, including sign-in events and audit records, that could show them more about who sent the email and from what session.

Understanding whether the sender authenticated into the account could rule out spoofing, but would not in itself provide proof that the sender used a corresponding password taken from an infostealer log, Hudson Rock noted. There are many ways to get around password-based authentication.

The researchers said that in any case where a credential is detected among infostealer logs, the organizations responsible for those accounts must contain them, revoke their access, rotate secrets, and go looking for suspicious activity.

"The disruption illustrates why credential exposure deserves attention beyond fraud and data theft," the researchers said.

"An account associated with an ordinary university user can become a means of reaching schools, frightening families, and consuming emergency resources."

The threats

Around 6,300 of Italy's 7,476 state schools received fake bomb threat emails between November 11-12, although only around 390 of them evacuated their respective buildings.

The emails contained messaging such as "we will annihilate you," and "we will carry out genocide against Italians," and mention of a "powerful explosive device… with a remote trigger."

Early reports suggested that the emails came from a Taiwanese email address and were signed by a "Mikhail Andropov, leader of the Vilayat of Misoginistan" – a fictitious state or region roughly mapping to "the land of Misogyny," with "vilayat" meaning an administrative region of the Ottoman Empire.

Various theories have been reported about the identity of the sender, ranging from a teacher based in the Philippines whose email was compromised to a Russia-backed disruption operation. Neither are confirmed. Russia denied any involvement.

Italy's Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said on Thursday evening that there was no credence to the emails, and that whoever was behind the coordinated hoax sought to invoke chaos across the country.

"To date, there is no evidence of a concrete danger," she said, ANSA reported. "These messages aren't intended to shock, they're intended to scare.

"Those who write them are primarily seeking our fear, wasted days, suspicion, and chaos. Investigators and the judiciary, along with their European colleagues, are working to determine who is behind them."

Schools in France, Ireland, Northern Ireland, and Scotland also received similar emails this week. None of the respective police forces believed the threats were legitimate.

Hundreds of schools across the Republic of Ireland received the emails, as did news organizations such as RTÉ, which evacuated its Donnybrook campus, disrupting scheduled programming.

Around 300 schools in Northern Ireland received bomb threats, although the PSNI said these were being treated as a hoax, and that the risk to the public was deemed low.

Likewise, Police Scotland confirmed around 1,000 schools were affected by the email campaign and that the threats weren’t believed to be credible.

In France, three school districts confirmed they received similar threats. Separately, domestic and international rail travel, including Eurostar services to London, were interrupted on Thursday following bomb threats made to Calais-Fréthun station.

The latest wave of threats follows similar happenings at other types of organizations in recent weeks, including airline operators, air traffic controllers, and blood banks.

At least 34 flights across various operators in Europe were affected earlier this month. Some were forced into unplanned landings, such as an Aer Lingus flight which pulled up to a French air base instead of its intended target of Rome.

Military fighter jets were also scrambled to escort others in Italian and Austrian airspace. ®

articles.title: HPE debuts hybrid storage configs: Rising SSD costs hit supercomputing
articles.text:
HPE is pitching high performance compute customers with hybrid configurations of its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems built for faster throughput, along with a Rack Management Controller that monitors cooling systems.

The hardware giant already supplies its Cray Supercomputing Storage Systems E2000 in all-flash, all-disk, tiered and hybrid configurations, but - we're told - the latest combination offers up to 41 percent more data throughput per storage rack.

The E2000 line embeds the Lustre open-source parallel file system, and is generally intended to fit NVMe Gen 5 solid-state drive (SSD) building blocks.

For the refreshed hybrid configurations, HPE is combining SSDs with new 32 TB SAS-4 (24 Gb/s SAS) HDDs and new enclosures supporting 74 or 100 drives.

HPE says it'll deliver up to 116 GB/s of read throughput and 92 GB/s of write throughput per rack, with up to 32 percent more usable storage capacity per rack for expansion to support the growing size of datasets in HPC, especially where sites are mixing AI and traditional simulation-style workloads.

One of the reasons behind these new hybrid configurations could be the ballooning cost of storage, caused by the relentless demand for AI infrastructure skewing the price of components such as memory and many other things. But prices for silicon-based NAND flash SSDs are growing faster than those of good old hard drives, as our colleagues at Blocks & Files reported.

HPE says that as demand for data-intensive workloads grows, prices for large SSDs have soared. The company claims the new hybrid configurations let research institutions and national laboratories spend less on storage and put that money toward compute node purchases, without giving up on the performance they need.

“When making long-term investments in environments where advanced workloads are rapidly evolving, our customers want scalable, dense, and flexible systems to help them address dynamic shifts in requirements," said Trish Damkroger, HPE senior veep for HPC and AI Infrastructure Solutions.

The latest hybrid configurations are expected to go on sale in early 2027.

HPE's other introduction is a Rack Management Controller, providing what HPE calls "intelligent liquid cooling” via real-time monitoring, leak detection and automated control features. It integrates with HPE Supercomputing Management Software to gather telemetry and provide control.

Several platform-specific versions will be offered, each tailored to different rack-scale systems. Support will launch with HPE's own Cray Supercomputing GX5000 infrastructure, naturally, with versions for Nvidia’s NVL72 and AMD’s Helion and Helios kit to follow.

The Rack Management Controller will be available for HPE’s kit in March 2027, with support for AMD and Nvidia expected to follow in June. ®

articles.title: Microsoft outage gives customers a crash course in dependence on Redmond
articles.text:
Microsoft 365 services are slowly recovering from a prolonged outage that has handed critics of single-vendor dependence a particularly unwelcome case study.

Ever wondered what it would be like if your IT supplier abruptly pulled the plug? Perhaps the result of a mood swing by an unpredictable political leader? For affected Microsoft customers, the disruption has offered an unwelcome preview. Email? Gone. Messaging with Teams? Iffy. Collaboration? Nope.

The list of problems in what Microsoft delicately called a "Service Degradation" is breathtaking. The company put the incident's start at 1826 GMT on November 12. Exchange Online fell over. Viewing recently used files in the Microsoft 365 application was problematic. Copilot threw a wobbly. Microsoft 365 Education was affected (unfortunate, considering the changes the company has made), and so on.

At 1401 GMT on November 13, Microsoft reported: "We're continuing to see improvements in service availability," but the damage has surely been done. If the outage halted work at your organization, then questions will have to be asked.

Even Microsoft's rivals had some sympathy for the engineers and administrators dealing with the problems.

Jos Poortvliet, co-founder of Nextcloud, told The Register: "Mistakes happen in the IT industry. This holds true for companies of all sizes, including us. Our heart goes out to all the admins today.

"This incident shows how dependent organizations are on a single ecosystem. Especially in critical infrastructure, monopolies are increasing the risk of stalling businesses globally if an incident occurs.

"When everything is hanging on a single vendor, companies can't switch providers quickly to get back up and running, or have a second setup as backup, or pull the plug when under attack and keep working air-gapped."

Similarly, Civo CEO Mark Boost noted that IT whoopsies were a way of life. "Every technology provider will experience failures," he said. "The real concern isn't that Microsoft has suffered an outage. It's that we've allowed so much of our critical infrastructure to become concentrated in the hands of so few companies, creating enormous single points of failure."

Dame Chi Onwurah, chair of the Commons Science and Technology Committee, also commented: "The global Microsoft outage only serves to highlight once again the lack of resilience in the UK's digital infrastructure, and the dangers that this dependency can pose to our security, economy and public services."

This week, Microsoft warned users to treat its unsupported Exchange Server 2016 and 2019 as "permanently vulnerable." Moving to Exchange Online brings its own dependencies, however. Beyond any compensation claims, Microsoft may face awkward conversations about those dependencies when contracts come up for renewal.

And there are alternatives. Although perhaps not so extreme as the measures overheard by one vulture in a German shared workspace: "Germany's love of the fax machine – we are finally getting our chance to shine! Our British colleagues cannot email; we have reverted to the natural way of the fax."

What a time to be alive. ®

articles.title: IIT Madras Advances Autonomous Shipping With New SEANAV Platform
articles.text:
Researchers at the Department of Ocean Engineering, Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Madras, have developed a real-time digital twin platform designed to test, validate, and train autonomous maritime navigation systems to help vessels navigate safely at sea.
Integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI), Virtual Reality (VR), and multi-sensor fusion, SEANAV constructs a virtual ocean environment where autonomous vessels can be evaluated before setting sail. Built on a Unity-based simulation engine, the platform recreates realistic ocean waves, dynamic shipping traffic, and adverse weather conditions, enabling ships to execute AI-driven collision avoidance and path-following manoeuvres.
The system allows multiple ships to navigate congested waterways simultaneously and offers an immersive VR interface for training maritime professionals. According to the institute, conducting thousands of hours of virtual simulation substantially reduces testing costs while promoting safer and more sustainable shipping operations.
The research has been published in the Journal of Offshore Mechanics and Arctic Engineering (ASME) and presented at ASME OMAE conferences in Vancouver and Tokyo.
Highlighting the importance of environmental perception in dynamic marine environments, researchers noted that existing maritime vision datasets, such as SeaShips and HRSC2016, lack sufficient variation in viewpoints and weather conditions, which limits the real-world reliability of deep learning models.
To overcome this, the team developed a novel custom dataset named ‘DetectShips’, comprising 14,000 real ship images, and combined it with the SeaShips dataset to train a computer vision algorithm integrated with stereo sensors.
Additionally, the researchers introduced ‘StereoLiD’, a hybrid sensing framework that combines stereo vision cameras with LiDAR data from the Unity simulation platform. While stereo cameras detect and classify vessels to estimate relative depth, LiDAR inputs further refine depth estimation accuracy. Data from both sensors are fused using a Kalman filter to achieve precise target localisation.
According to the researchers, this multi-vision sensor fusion overcomes common limitations of conventional optical sensors, including fluctuating lighting conditions and dense fog, ensuring dependable target detection and navigation across complex oceanic environments.

articles.title: Another Linux kernel developer steps back from some duties due to overload
articles.text:
Arm's Lorenzo Stoakes isn't quitting Linux kernel development, though he's stepping back from some of the patch-review work he used to handle.

Stoakes is a principal software engineer at Arm and he's a busy chap. Aside from writing the forthcoming book The Linux Memory Manager, in his CV [PDF], he says:

"I hold four maintainerships: memory mapping, memory mapping (locking), memory mapping (madvise) – essentially the entirety of the userland API to memory management – and the reverse mapping which connects physical to virtual memory."

Even so, he plans to soon be doing a little less. Earlier this week he posted an email to the Linux kernel mailing list to say that he was planning to drop some of his workload.

He explained:

"Given the current throughput in the kernel resulting from AI-generated series, I unfortunately lack the bandwidth to generally be able to offer review except in those areas I maintain. […] Apologies for doing this, but given the current trends I'd like to do something to make my inbox a little more manageable."

As it happens, this came just the day after the Paramount Penguin himself said that he saw signs that the AI patch tide was "starting to turn."

Stoakes told The Register:

"I am retaining my maintainerships and have no plans on giving those up, I just want my inbox to be less horrendous.

"And yeah, AI is part of the reason; in general, it's gone from 'once a week' to 'daily' to 'half of what I see in review'.

"But the AI wave is hitting [memory management] across the board, really."

He added:

"I have a habit of burning myself out over weekends and evenings – you can see my involvement on a thread talking about that here - which gives you a sense of my views if you read back through that thread."

At the Open Source Summit last month, the Reg FOSS desk joined the "Ask the Expert" session with Greg Kroah-Hartman, and he too expressed worrying sentiments:

"The onslaught of the LLM-generated patches… we don't have enough people to review them all… We need more reviewers. We don't have enough. All of the maintainers are burnt out, and we have been for ten years."

Kroah-Hartman also said:

"I want to go down to two Long Term Support releases – four, maximum. Six is too many. We're too busy. We don't have the manpower. It’s crazy."

On Red Hat's model of offering 10 years of support for products with a given version of the kernel:

"Debian does it right. Debian and Yocto run the world. I've argued for years that the RHEL and SLES model is broken. That's why I don't work for SUSE any more." ®

articles.text:
Gunsmiths from Darra Adam Khel, Pakistan have shown off a home-made rifle that appears to closely resemble India’s INSAS assault rifle. However, it is said to be chambered in .308 cal rather than INSAS’ 5.56x45mm rounds. The rifle can be seen in images appearing to be a traditional assault rifle with fixed shoulder stock, large handguard and curved magazine. While the general shape, especially of the receiver, stock and handguard do appear similar to the Indian version, some design differences can be seen which would suggest it may be a local modification.
The most interesting feature is the claim it is chambered in .308. The original INSAS design was developed using the 5.56x45mm NATO round and was introduced into Indian military service during the 1990s. To produce a rifle chambered in .308 Winchester or the similar 7.62x51mm NATO would require a completely different design, with modifications to the receiver, bolt system and magazine.
The larger round would also need modifications to the workings of the rifle. This means that it cannot be simply considered a conversion of the original INSAS rifle, and would likely be a completely different design.
Darra Adam Khel, situated within Pakistan’s Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province, is well known for being a centre of small arms production. Many workshops will produce and modify firearms, such as assault rifles, pistols and shotguns. Often they take inspiration from different manufacturers.
While seeing an INSAS style rifle is interesting and shows how Indian military designs can draw attention, this does not mean it is a licensed design or that the manufacturer had access to the original INSAS blueprints.
There is no independent confirmation on who made the rifle, what the internal workings are like, what calibre it is and how it performs. There is no public information on how many were made or what they were intended for.

articles.title: It's the end of the world as we know it, per a physicist's 1960 prediction
articles.text:
As of this morning, Microsoft is still scrambling to restore service following yesterday's global outage, with millions of users unable to access Outlook and other vital tools. It's not the end of the world, but it does seem fitting that this should happen on the day a physicist predicted would be the end of humanity: November 13, 2026. And it falls on a Friday, too. The physicist in question is Heinz von Foerster, who published a 1960 paper in the journal Science predicting that by today, overpopulation would reach the breaking point.

It's not a new fear. English economist Thomas Malthus—one of the early pioneers in modeling population dynamics—made a similar prediction in 1798, claiming that a rapidly growing population would eventually exhaust the available food supply, and humanity would starve to death. His model rested on the assumption of exponential growth, but the equation is only applicable under specific conditions, such as scientists growing bacteria in a lab in a perfectly controlled environment. Even then, while growth occurs exponentially for a time, it does not continue forever.

Population dynamics are notoriously tricky to calculate because there are so many variables to consider and so much unpredictability in the system. In his 1960 analysis, Von Foerster accurately measured past trends in population growth, but like Malthus, he assumed those trends would carry into the future largely unchanged. So he projected that human population growth would march inexorably toward infinity. We wouldn't starve to death; von Foerster thought we would be ingenious enough to solve the food supply problem. Instead, "they will be squeezed to death," he wrote.

articles.title: Most affairs don't matter except to the people involved. Ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen's blunder will rock the world
articles.text:
It's a story as old as time. Billionaire nerd boy meets girl. Girl is later suspected of being a spy. News at 11. Oh, and it's also been reported that he was having an affair with one of his direct-report employees. When Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang makes a "romantic" blunder, he doesn't do it halfway.

The boss of the world's most valuable company – well, it was until recently, anyway – publicly resigned yesterday, November 12, as CEO, president, and board member, effective immediately. We don't know if he jumped or if he was pushed.

He left after admitting to having an affair. Although he never named an affair partner, one of the affairs was reported to be with Alice Huang, AKA Huang Le. She's head of the Chinese company Megaspeed, which was an Nvidia partner. Megaspeed is accused of being a front for China's government that was used to transfer Nvidia chips to China, although this hasn't been proven. Some US officials also suspect [PDF] she's working for Chinese intelligence, although the DoJ said it hasn't yet reached a conclusion about this. The final nail in Jensen's coffin came when The New York Times reported he had also allegedly had an affair with Nvidia's VP of health care, Kimberly Powell. Jeeze, guy!

In the aftermath, Nvidia's CFO, Colette Kress, was appointed interim CEO. She won't, I suspect, be in the job for long. CFOs are not CEOs. The jobs aren't remotely the same. In most companies, Huang would be replaced by the COO. That can't happen here. Nvidia doesn't have a COO. Both inside and outside of Nvidia, Huang is seen as Nvidia, and Nvidia as Huang.

These days, billionaire CEOs are perceived as God-kings who know all and rule all. Much more often than not, that's BS.

That isn't the case with Nvidia. Huang co-founded Nvidia on April 5, 1993. He was appointed CEO on day one, and he never left the job. At first, the company staggered forward. When it released the GeForce 256 in 1999, which it marketed as the first GPU, it started on its path to becoming the chip manufacturer of choice for PC gamers. It still is today.

That's a great niche, but it doesn't make a company a trillion-dollar business. No, the path to that dizzying height came when, in 2006, Nvidia unveiled CUDA. This programming architecture opened its GPUs' parallel-processing capabilities to scientific and other non-graphics workloads. From there, CUDA would become the foundation for most high-performance and AI computing.

Huang was at the center of it all. He still was until now. At KubeCon North America, the trade show for Kubernetes, used in well over half of all AI projects, I spoke to many Nvidia employees. There were two things they all mentioned. First, they were in a state of shock. Maybe the top brass and government officials both in China and the US knew Huang was fooling with fire; the developer rank-and-file folks I spoke to hadn't had a clue. The second was that every month, Huang held an all-hands meeting where, instead of a per-forma corporate pep rally, he answered questions from everyone and gave them real answers. He knew his technology well and actually led his company instead of just impressing gullible stock buyers.

Nvidia can't replace him. It really can't. I'm reminded of when John Sculley forced Steve Jobs out at Apple in 1985. If you're not old enough to remember, Apple did fine for a while, but then by the mid-90s, it lost its way. Apple got its mojo back, and started its rise to being one of the world's top companies only after Jobs came back in 1996.

The big difference, of course, is that Huang's not coming back. I heard many people say that Huang was "too big to fail." True, morality no longer matters much in the US – see Trump's kleptocracy – but this is different. Huang betrayed not just his wife, but his board, employees, and stockholders. If, as some suspect, the board knew full well what was going on, they should be tossed out too, but that's a story for another day.

Oh, and as for Trump's suggestions that Apple's former CEO Tim Cook should become Nvidia's CEO? Give me a break.

Now the question of the day is: how can Nvidia recover from this blow? I don't think it can. I used to say that I didn't know where the AI companies were going, but I was sure that so long as capital kept flowing into Big AI, Nvidia was the one company you could count on that would make money. I think I was wrong.

What does that mean? In the short term, Nvidia stock, after dropping 14 percent in early trading on Thursday, is down "only" five percent. Despite all the Sturm und Drang over Huang's departure, the NASDAQ is actually, when I wrote this, up. Even Nvidia's bonds are holding steady.

Amazon and Google, which have their own horses in the AI TPU races, are hoping, of course, that Nvidia's misfortune will help them lever open the AI hardware market. In these early hours, I don't see that happening.

Frankly, I'm amazed at how stockowners are shaking off Huang's resignation. The AI fever dream, for now, is continuing unabated.

That said, can this go on? This irrational exuberance rests on the belief that, no matter what happens, AI will continue to rule the stock market. Eventually, though, the bubble may pop, and that could put some strain on the global economy. For now, people are ignoring how bad this blow is, or perhaps they're not aware of it.

In a few years, I expect Huang's affair will be seen as the first needle in the AI bubble. ®

articles.title: Indian Army MRSAM Launcher Spotted in Bengaluru Traffic
articles.text:
An image of an Indian Army Medium Range Surface-to-Air Missile (MRSAM) mobile launcher has been captured on camera while being transported on the Outer Ring Road (ORR) in Bengaluru. This gives a look into one of the top systems within India’s air defence capabilities. This mobile launcher is used to defend military assets using its ability to shoot down aircraft, helicopters, UAVs and missiles.
This appears to be part of the Medium Range Surface-to-Air Missile (MRSAM) Mobile Launcher System (MLS) used by the Army. However it is just a small subsection of the overall system.
The Armies Medium Range Surface-to-Air Missile (MRSAM) has been developed in collaboration between the Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO) and Israel Aerospace Industries (IAI). It is produced by Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL) as the prime contractor. Along with many Indian public and private sector companies.
The Mobile Launcher System (MLS) for the MRSAM is produced by Tata Advanced Systems. Technical information states that this launcher consists of a mobile platform with the Launch Control System, communication systems and up to 8 canisterised missiles. It also contains its own power generation and a high communication mast.
The full Medium Range Surface-to-Air Missile (MRSAM) system consists of Missiles, Combat Management System (CMS), Mobile Launcher Systems, Advanced Long Range Radar, Mobile Power Systems, Radar Power Systems, Reloader Vehicles and Field Service Vehicles. All working to detect, track, prioritise and engage aerial threats.
The MRSAM is a point and area defence system. It can engage aerial threats up to around 70km away. It can engage several targets in complex saturation environments. The system is meant to be used to shoot down fighter jets, helicopters, UAVs as well as guided and unguided weapons. It can also engage subsonic and supersonic cruise missiles.
This missile uses an indigenously developed rocket motor and a highly manoeuvrable control system. The system is network able to allow the individual components to work together to create an air defence system.
The Army variant of the system had its first successful flight test back in December 2020. During this test the missile engaged a high speed aerial target at the Integrated Test Range in Chandipur, Odisha. Since then tests have shown that the system can engage various aerial targets. The Indian Army are now looking to deploy the system.
This image also shows how many companies are involved in producing missiles for India. Whilst BDL are responsible for missile integration, the launcher and other parts of the system contain specialist products from companies like Tata Advanced Systems.

Climate Action Tracker, a nonprofit group that analyzes climate policies, found that the planet is still on track to warm nearly 5° Fahrenheit by 2100, a rise that would devastate coral reefs, disrupt agriculture and forests and melt most of the world’s ice. In a separate bulletin, the European Union’s Copernicus climate change service reported that global warming has accelerated significantly since the 2015 Paris climate agreement.

When the Paris agreement was adopted, the average global temperature was projected to surpass the pact’s long-term threshold of 2.7° Fahrenheit above the preindustrial average around 2045. articles.title: Oh my Word! Microsoft retires compatibility options, because who needs layouts to stay put
articles.text:
Microsoft is retiring some legacy layout settings in Word, potentially rearranging documents created or last saved in Word 2010 or earlier.

"Affected documents may show layout differences, such as text reflow, changes in spacing or page count, or images and shapes moving to another page," the Windows biz said.

The advice, if silly little things like page layout in a document matter, is to "consider exporting it to PDF before the change."

Compatibility Mode lets a newer version of Word open a document created in an older version, such as Word 2010, without changing its layout. Newer features are switched off while the document is open this way. Users can convert the document to unlock newer features, although people using older versions of Word may then have difficulty editing parts of it.

Microsoft has not identified the individual settings being retired, saying only: "We are retiring a set of compatibility options in Microsoft Word (desktop app) for documents in Compatibility Mode." The reason? "To simplify how Word handles document layout and provide a more consistent experience across platforms."

Administrators may therefore want to check older templates, forms, and other documents whose pagination needs to stay put.

The change is due to begin rolling out in the Windows version of Word from December 2026 and be completed by January 2027. The Mac version will follow in early 2027.

Microsoft Word is more than 40 years old, and its first Windows version was released as the 1980s drew to a close. The word processor has evolved over the decades and is a mainstay of Microsoft's productivity suite.

Compatibility Mode helps keep older documents from having their layouts abruptly borked the way Word does so well. Losing some of those safeguards could give administrators a fresh batch of "what the heck has happened to this document?" tickets as the change rolls out. ®

Overall this shows that India’s sea based nuclear deterrent is entering a more challenging stage. articles.title: Quantum Systems drones back in the air after malware scare
articles.text:
Quantum Systems says its drones are flying again with Germany's military after a cyberattack prompted a precautionary grounding.

The company says it spotted the attack at the end of October and reported it to the relevant authorities, but disclosed few details about the intrusion.

"The threat was contained thanks to the swift response of our IT and security teams in close and transparent collaboration with the authorities," it said on Thursday.

"Through the quick measures taken and the characteristics of the incident, there is no risk in operating Quantum Systems' unmanned systems for the end users and the operators."

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?

—Aaron Zamost, a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square

The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley have built careers claiming to see the future. Yet five weeks before the midterms, many gathered at the White House to pose with Trump and endorse his “Super Intelligence” agenda, despite growing opposition to AI and data centers.

Their decision to lash themselves to President Trump was a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment. 

Here’s why Silicon Valley’s tech leaders may be less visionary than they think.

Nvidia privately confirmed it could track chips to fight smuggling, even as industry publicly questioned feasibility

Nvidia representatives told Illinois representative Bill Foster that it was possible to implement the anti-smuggling measures called for in the Chip Security Act, Foster told MIT Technology Review on Thursday, despite an industry group claiming they were “potentially infeasible.”

Foster, a Democrat who serves on the Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, is a cosponsor of the act, which would introduce geotracking requirements to verify the location of advanced AI chips and prevent their smuggling to China.

The act is drawing renewed attention following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and reported affair. Find out what the proposed tracking measures would involve.

—James O’Donnell

More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials

Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can control robotic limbs and computers, and even “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of these devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014.

He’s been working on a set of guidelines for ethical trials to respect participants’ autonomy—and access their own brain data whenever they want.

Read the full story on the push to give volunteers in brain implant trials more rights.

articles.title: Palantir adds three UK police forces to its beat with £10.1M deal
articles.text:
Three UK police forces led by Cambridgeshire Constabulary have awarded Palantir a £10.1 million contract after London Mayor Sadiq Khan blocked a separate deal with the Metropolitan Police.

The five-year agreement covers Bedfordshire Police, Cambridgeshire Constabulary, and Hertfordshire Constabulary, despite warnings from campaigners and politicians about dependence on the supplier.

A contract award notice says the east of England police forces expect the Palantir platform to provide "an enterprise-wide data integration and analytics capability, enabling the secure ingestion, linking, and analysis of data from multiple systems and sources across the policing environment." The contract runs until October 2031, with the estimated value covering all three forces.

News of the award coincided with revelations that former Metropolitan Police commissioner Dame Cressida Dick has worked as a paid adviser to Palantir since September 2025.

A Palantir spokesperson told the Bureau of Investigative Journalism: "Dame Cressida is advising us on how our software could help improve the delivery of services in the public sector, drawing on more than 40 years of public service in a variety of roles."

Dick said her role was limited to advising on how such products could assist public services. She said she had never lobbied or advocated for Palantir, or introduced the company to her contacts.

Dick led the Metropolitan Police, the UK's largest force, between 2017 and 2022. She left after Khan said he had lost confidence in her. She later said she was "intimidated" into leaving.

Separately, Khan stepped in to block the Met from awarding a £50 million contract to Palantir. His office cited serious concerns about the procurement process. Palantir later sued the Met, but the case was settled in October.

The new police contract award follows a report from MPs warning of vendor lock-in to US suppliers, including Palantir. It said: "Our view that Palantir's increasing presence across the public sector represents an unacceptable point of weakness is not ideologically motivated or driven by concerns about the quality of their products.

"The government should retain the ability to pick and choose individual suppliers and safeguard against the risk of vendor lock-in and debilitating dependencies, particularly in areas of critical national importance such as healthcare and national security infrastructure." ®

articles.title: BOFH: The best way to stop an idea spreading is a controlled burn
articles.text:
Look, off in the ether – is it a bird, is it a plane? No, it's a stupid idea, on final approach...

And look, the Boss has his office door open!

C L E A R A N C E T O L A N D !

...

The Boss has wandered into Mission Control with something obviously on his mind. Over time, the PFY and I have learned to equate these thoughtful moments with the BAG FULL lamp of a commercial vacuum cleaner at a waxing salon. Do not open.

His presence in Mission Control is never a good sign, but his "thoughtful" presence, even more so. He'll have seen something, read something, spoken to someone, or possibly overheard something in a toilet stall that will have sounded – to him – like a great idea. Or it might have been a cheddar-frenzy-induced fever dream that he wants to run by us.

And the Boss's crazy ideas are, unfortunately, like bran flakes to his mental digestion, the output of which being delivered to the PFY and myself as a veritable slurry of poorly considered ideas.

"AI," he says, pausing for effect, once he's rolled to a stop.

He then waits patiently for one of us to ask "What about AI?" However, that will never happen. In terms of stupidity, it's up there with saying Candyman into a mirror five times, power washing a gremlin, or visiting a basement when Jason's in town.

...

"For the security system," the Boss teases.

I continue my intense focus on my monitors, hoping the lunacy will depart. The PFY does the same.

The PFY and I know that the only way out of this is to stall till the end of the day, at which time the Boss's overnight reset will trigger, leaving him only a vague memory of having had a good idea.

>clickety< >tap<

"Uh-oh," I say, reaching into my drawer for my crashtop. "It looks like one of the distribution switches on 4 has crashed."

>tappity<

"And not just 4 – it looks like the boardroom has gone down too."

"It could be a virus," I say, using words I know the Boss will respond to.

"A virus?!" the Boss gasps.

"I don't know. It's too soon to tell," I say, departing.

...

So now I'm hiding in a cramped comms room on the fourth floor while I plug the crashtop into the CCTV VLAN so I can check on the Boss's location. Luckily, we upgraded the system to an AI-integrated platform, so I only need to type IDIOT into the search field to find him.

Sure enough, he's back in his office, typing away furiously, which can only mean there's a memo on its way. And if there's a memo, there's a path to reminding him of his dumb idea tomorrow...

>tappity< >tap< >tap< >clickety<

On the screen, the Boss looks around anxiously as his laptop fires up DBAN in full confirm mode. He then reaches for a sheet of paper and starts scribbling furiously.

>tappity< >tap<

The office lights switch off as the BMS system clock suddenly finds out that it's midnight.

On the screen, the Boss's phone torch comes on and he resumes scribbling.

>bip< >bip< >bip< >biiiiiiip<

>ring<

"Hello?" the Boss asks, with a hint of feedback.

"It's the virus!" I gasp. "It's coming from inside the building!!!"

Meantime, I've messaged the PFY and advised him to pick up the shredder from the boardroom cupboard.

"What do I do?" the Boss gasps.

"It's the wireless broadband connection on the roof!" I say. "We need to disconnect it!"

"I thought you said it was coming from inside the building?" the Boss asks.

DAMMIT!

>tappity< >click< >tap< >tap<

Further discussion is impossible now that his phone is erasing itself, having been marked as a stolen device...

The PFY was unable to find the shredder, as it looks to have been dumped now that board papers are no longer printed. On the plus side, he has a plan.

...two hours later...

"So, we're clear to enter the building?" I ask the fire warden.

"Yes, you're clear, though it looks like the fire started on your floor."

"It doesn't surprise me," I say. "We're creative people. Our ideas spark innovation."

"It looks like there was some as-yet-unknown accelerant used."

"Really? Was it... enthusiasm?" I ask.

"No, more like lighter fluid."

"Oh," I say, thinking of the smokers the PFY occasionally chats to outside at the skip. "Well, we may never know."

"Don't you have some sort of AI surveillance system?" he asks.

"Sadly, that was the first thing to go," I lie.

...Later, in Mission Control...

"So, in review," the PFY says. "We shut down a couple of switches, put the building in night mode, trashed a laptop and a mobile phone, then set fire to the building."

"Yes."

"Simply to stop a dumb idea?"

"Yes."

"And the funny thing is, I took a look at his scribblings – and it wasn't all that bad."

"Really?" I ask, reaching for the isopropyl and a lighter, just in case it's contagious.

articles.title: Crackdown on UK medical record snooping after staff reported sneaking 300+ times this year
articles.text:
Britain's privacy watchdog has put healthcare bosses on notice after receiving more than 300 reports of staff snooping through medical records this year, demanding that executives personally confirm they're doing enough to keep prying eyes out of patient files.

The Information Commissioner's Office (ICO) said on Thursday that it had written to more than 200 senior health leaders across the UK, warning that employees accessing records without good reason put patient privacy and public trust at risk.

The ICO received and assessed more than 300 reports of medical record snooping between January and mid-October 2026. Staff were caught looking up people they knew, poking around patient files out of sheer curiosity, and sharing private information with people who had no business seeing it.

The figure covers reports submitted by healthcare organizations rather than confirmed breaches, and excludes cases still awaiting assessment.

ICO chief executive Paul Arnold wants health bosses to personally assure him that their organizations have safeguards in place to stop staff having a nose through records they aren't supposed to see.

"Accessing someone's health records without a legitimate reason isn't harmless curiosity. It can cause enormous distress to patients and jeopardize the vital trust people place in our health service," Arnold said.

In a three-page letter to chief executives, Arnold makes clear that simply trusting staff to behave themselves won't cut it. He wants to know who can access patient records, whether anyone is checking what they're looking at, and what happens when somebody gets caught snooping.

Health bosses are also expected to investigate suspected breaches without dragging their feet, work out whether patients need to be told, and take action against staff caught accessing records they shouldn't.

Executives have until November 27 to respond. Those who haven't reviewed their safeguards in the past six months, or aren't happy with what they find, have been given another three months to put their house in order.

The problem isn't necessarily that healthcare workers are hacking into systems, as many already have legitimate access to patient records as part of their jobs. The trouble starts when they use that access to look up someone they're not treating, whether it's a neighbor, an ex-partner, or somebody whose name has appeared in the news.

This isn't the first time health authorities have tried to stamp out the problem. In July, NHS England warned employees that accessing records without a legitimate reason could cost them their jobs or even land them in prison.

That crackdown followed incidents involving staff accessing the medical records of victims of high-profile crimes, including the Nottingham attacks. NHS England also published guidance encouraging organizations to use access controls and audit systems to catch employees poking around where they shouldn't.

Some newer electronic patient record systems can even flag suspicious access in real time, although the NHS acknowledged that monitoring capabilities vary depending on the technology organizations have installed.

The scale of the problem has been troubling regulators for years. In July, the UK government told Parliament that 1,445 cases of inappropriate access had been reported to the ICO between 2019 and 2025.

And the consequences can go beyond getting the sack. The ICO has prosecuted 16 healthcare workers for snooping through patient records over the past decade, with unauthorized access to personal information potentially amounting to a criminal offense under the Data Protection Act 2018.

Arnold warned that the regulator could also take enforcement action against healthcare organizations whose protections aren't up to scratch.

"I've written to chief executives across the UK asking them to personally assure me that their safeguards work in practice. Where they don't, we expect organizations to put that right," he said.

With hundreds of reports already landing on the watchdog's desk this year, healthcare bosses now have a fortnight to explain how they're keeping staff out of records they have no business reading. ®

articles.title: Brit police watchdog says cops' use of facial recog risks wrongful arrests
articles.text:
UK police forces must do more to prevent the wrongful arrests of people subjected to retrospective facial recognition (RFR) searches, according to a Criminal Justice Inspectorate that holds deep concerns about the way in which the technology is used.

According to a report from His Majesty's Inspectorate of Constabulary and Fire & Rescue Services (HMICFRS), there is a large gap in understanding among police forces and the National Crime Agency about how RFR should be used in responsible policing.

The inspectorate blamed "fragmented and underdeveloped" frameworks for governance and legislation.

It pointed to a lack of bespoke legislation to provide a uniform approach to police facial recognition use – and said existing laws have not kept pace with the technology. HMICFRS also said the rules governing each force's use of RFR are mismatched, and called for a statutory code to be included in the forthcoming Police Reform Bill to set nationwide standards.

Illustrating the breadth of misunderstanding across forces, the report noted that despite the message being routinely communicated by National Police Chiefs' Council (NPCC) reps, individual investigators "often" thought RFR results constituted evidence rather than intelligence.

In many cases, they are unaware that RFR results require further enquiries before enforcement action can be taken.

"We found that some investigators didn't always carry out enough corroborative enquiries before acting on potential matches," the report stated. "In a small number of cases, officers relied too heavily on RFR results, which led to inappropriate investigative action.

"Although some forces had strengthened their processes after such incidents, practice remained inconsistent."

Later in the report, the inspectorate described the findings as "deeply concerning."

Some of the excuses police staff offered included acute demands on response teams leading to reduced opportunities to carry out further enquiries before acting on RFR matches. In one force, managers were known to encourage officers to "progress investigations quickly" after getting a match on the RFR system.

However, the inspectorate clarified that just because an arrest is made, it does not necessarily mean it is wrongful, as investigators may need to rule out subjects from their inquiries.

The onus for taking action should also be placed on the police forces themselves, given that some lack formal procedures regarding how RFR enquiries should be carried out, the report noted.

The best forces had centralized facial recognition teams, which generally provided better governance and consistent processes.

Officials fear long-term misuse of RFR, and other forms of facial recognition, will erode public trust in the technology, which it insists remains generally high.

Surveys carried out in 2025 by the likes of the Ada Lovelace Institute and Alan Turing Institute, as well as the King's College London Policy Institute, showed a generally favorable view of facial recognition use in UK policing, with support ranging from 91 percent and 53 percent respectively.

Home Office figures released on Thursday to complement the report show similar positivity toward the technology among police officers, with only 4 percent reporting a negative experience.

The Register's comments section often paints a vastly different picture of public perception of facial recognition.

Kathryn Stone, his majesty's inspector at HMICFRS, said facial recognition has transformed policing, allowing officers to compare images in seconds, allowing them to solve crimes more quickly, but echoed the report's main concerns.

"Police forces must be able to show that appropriate safeguards are in place, risks relating to bias and data retention are effectively managed, and decisions are still subject to human judgment," she said.

"A clearer statutory framework, stronger national standards and improved governance and oversight arrangements are essential to maintaining public confidence."

As well as legislative and governance-related concerns, HMICFRS also noted in its report that officers' training around the use of RFR remains inconsistent, and if improvements were made, this would lead to more effective and lawful use of RFR across the UK.

Another major issue was police forces' failure to meet their image retention obligations. Forces were found too often to retain custody images taken of suspects on the Police National Database, against which many RFR queries are made.

Police guidance sets out the scenarios in which custody images can and cannot be retained, and the inspectorate found that forces have failed to delete images that should have been wiped.

The Police Reform Bill includes a provision to group custody images with the likes of DNA and fingerprints, bringing about more robust measures to ensure they are retained or deleted in line with legal requirements.

A Home Office review previously found in 2017 that introducing such a statutory framework was untenable. It concluded that police could not automate the deletion of these images, and doing so manually would be too time-consuming.

Jasleen Chaggar, senior legal and policy officer at Big Brother Watch, said UK police cannot be allowed to continue to use RFR when it risks wrongfully arresting individuals.

"The revelations that officers are treating facial recognition as bona fide evidence rather than a probability score is alarming," she said.

"This approach significantly increases the risk that more innocent people will have officers knock on their door to arrest them for crimes committed in towns they've never visited, as we've seen before.

"Worse still, police aren't even logging their use of retrospective facial recognition, meaning people could wrongfully become suspects in criminal investigations without any record of why they've been accused."

Chaggar called on the government to "urgently step in" and help the UK's police forces to sort out the new frameworks needed for effective RFR use. ®

articles.title: More autonomy, fewer NDAs: Volunteers have new requests for brain implant trials
articles.text:
Scientists have been working on ways to decode brain activity for decades. Teams have developed brain implants that can be used to control robotic limbs and computers, and even to “speak.”

The people who volunteer for trials of those devices play a vital role in that research, and they ought to be recognized for their contributions, says Ian Burkhart, who had one implanted in his own brain back in 2014. He’s been working on a set of guidelines for researchers developing brain-computer interfaces (BCIs).

Ethics guidelines for clinical trials already exist. But BCI trials are different, says Jennifer Chandler, a professor of law and neuroethics at the University of Ottawa who also worked on the guidelines. “These are people who have a device embedded in their brain, are in trials sometimes for years and years … [and contribute] a significant investment of time, of the body, and of intellectual effort.”

Burkhart was left paralyzed from the chest down following a diving accident in 2010, when he was 19 years old. Around four years later, he volunteered to become the first person to trial a brain implant designed for hand control.

He had an array of 96 electrodes inserted into the part of his brain that controls movement. The electrodes were connected to a computer via a cable that essentially plugged into his head. Algorithms on the computer were designed to interpret those signals and deliver them to another sleeve of electrodes worn on Burkhart’s arm, allowing him to control it.

The first movements were small, but Burkhart was ultimately able to use the system to pour beads from bottles, move small and delicate objects, and even play Guitar Hero, if only during lab visits. It was a scientific breakthrough.

Burkhart took part in two years-long clinical trials over the seven-and-a-half-year period he had the electrode array implanted in his brain. “It was a fantastic experience,” he says. “But there’s certainly some things that, knowing what I know now, I would want to do a little differently.”

In 2022, Burkhart cofounded BCI Pioneers Coalition—an organization through which people who have taken part in BCI trials can share their experiences, both with each other and with researchers. Over the last year, members of the group have been developing a set of guidelines based on those experiences. The idea is to help academics, clinicians, and companies run ethical trials that respect participants’ autonomy.

The guidelines, published on Tuesday, lay out a list of recommendations that fall within 13 categories. One, for example, focuses on recognizing and compensating trial participants. During the trials that Burkhart participated in, “I was going into the lab two or three days a week, for four hours at a time,” he recalls. “That’s [easily] a part-time job if you just count the hours you’re putting in.”

As the trial progressed, Burkhart says, he learned more and was able to give more constructive feedback on what was working and what wasn’t. He says he was a key member of the research team. Others who find themselves in a similar position might appreciate being listed as a coauthor on scientific publications or publicly named as a research collaborator, he says. Burkhart and his colleagues acknowledge that not everyone will want this, however.  

The guidelines also address the thorny question of privacy. That’s important: The public will always be interested in cutting-edge biotechnologies like these—and the guidelines say researchers also have a duty to prepare participants for the possibility of media attention. In some cases, it might be difficult to completely conceal the identity of trial participants.

Things get even more complicated when it comes to the privacy of participants’ brain data. Research teams will need to access, analyze, and—at least temporarily—store this data. Burkhart wasn’t too bothered about that in his case, where scientists were collecting neural activity related to movement. But people who have brain implants designed for turning thoughts into words might feel differently. 

The guidelines state that brain data “should be understood as the participant’s personal information.” They are pushing for participants to be able to access their own brain data whenever they want—something that has not always been possible—and want to make sure people aren’t prevented from sharing it with their own doctors because of embargoes or nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) designed to keep findings under wraps from competitors.

“It’s not super common for there to be firm NDAs within a lot of the trials,” says Burkhart. “But it’s something where we want to make sure that that does not happen.”

The guidelines also address what comes after a trial. Around five years after Burkhart had his device implanted, the research team ran into some issues with funding. When we last spoke a few years ago, he recalled how he was told he would have to have the implant removed and could have it put back in once the team had secured funding. (And we’re talking about brain surgery here.)

Ultimately, he kept the implant until 2021, when it was removed after an infection started to develop at the point where the cable led into his scalp. But losing the device after all those years was difficult; he’d regained the ability to move his arm—and then lost it again.

Rita Leggett, an Australian woman who had a device implanted in her brain to treat her epilepsy, has said she felt she “became one” with her implant. When the company that made it went bust two years later, the device was removed against her will—an act ethicists have described as a potential breach of human rights.

Researchers should instead commit to maintaining brain devices for a “reasonable period” after a trial ends, according to the guidelines. Participants should be given plenty of time to prepare for the surgery to remove it. And researchers should set aside extra funds to support trial participants who have to do that.

Some of the guidelines are vague and may overlap with existing ethics standards. They don’t all spell out explicit solutions. They were also developed with feedback from a small group of individuals—the number of people living with BCIs is still very low. The team hopes to grow and expand on the guidelines over time. Burkhart also plans to discuss them with researchers at an upcoming neuroscience conference.

“This is a living document, and this is version one,” says Chandler. “It’s just the starting point.”
